summary: Mission Design Lab is a browser game where students design, launch and fly a complete space mission, from concept to operation. Players choose a destination (Earth orbit, the Moon or Mars) and a science objective. They then build the spacecraft (instruments, power, communications, propulsion), pick a launch vehicle within a budget, and must pass a Flight Readiness Poll that checks seven mission requirements. During launch, cruise and operations they make time-limited decisions, such as holding the count for an anvil cloud or reacting to a solar storm, and each choice moves real mass, power, data, Δv and cost margins. A mission report explains what worked, what failed and why. It replays each mission over 200 seeded re-flights to separate good design from luck, and links each lesson to real NASA missions and sources. Mission design concepts stay abstract in a classroom. This game makes them tangible: students feel why a heavier instrument needs a bigger launcher and a bigger budget. It runs in any browser with no install and no account.
details:
What it does: the player runs a mission through five stages.

1. Choose and brief: a destination and a science objective, which set the mission requirements.

2. Design: launcher, power, communications, propulsion and instruments on a live 3D spacecraft, with six live margins (budget, mass vs launcher, power, Δv, data downlink, instruments).

3. Readiness: a GO/NO-GO poll on requirements R1-R7. The player can fix a flagged item or launch with the risk.

4. Launch and fly: a real-time ascent with weather holds, hold-down clamps, Max-Q, staging, MECO/SECO, then cruise and operations decision cards (solar storms, conjunctions, eclipses, radiation).

5. Report: outcome, score, expected-versus-actual over 200 seeded re-flights, a mission timeline, concepts learned, a short quiz, and real historical cases with sources.

How it works: a deterministic, seeded simulation built on real engineering relationships:

- Rocket equation (Δv = Isp·g₀·ln(m₀/m_f)), Earth's rotation boost by launch latitude, and orbit and transfer costs.

- Additive power budgets, eclipse losses, data rates, radiation and thermal limits.

- Guided mode (2 revives) and Expert mode (1 revive).

Benefits and impact: students experience the whole mission, where each choice moves every other budget, instead of meeting each topic separately in class. Every decision shows its "why", and real missions (Apollo 12 lightning, Atlas/Centaur-67, Mars Climate Orbiter and others) connect the game to real spaceflight history.

Tools: TypeScript, Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, three.js (WebGL 3D with custom shaders), reka-ui, Vitest and Playwright (over 700 unit tests plus end-to-end tests), and Vercel static hosting with a Content Security Policy. Saves stay in the player's browser.

Creativity: the real spacecraft and rocket stand in a 3D scene that changes as you design. Launch decisions are based on real launch rules. A "Real or render?" quiz sets NASA photos next to our renders. Our pitch runs inside the game itself.

Factors considered: scientific accuracy at a student level, the reason made visible for every choice, accessibility (keyboard, phone layout, reduced motion), and no install or account so it works in any classroom.

Use of SI: AI coding assistants (Claude) were used to help write code, tests and documentation. All game design, physics choices and sources were checked by the team.
